node.label: Alessandro Portelli
node.date_label: 1981 The Peculiarities of Oral History · 1991 The Death of Luigi Trastulli and Other Stories · 1997 The Battle of Valle Giulia
node.description: Alessandro Portelli examines oral testimony as an encounter that produces historical evidence. His studies of Italian workers and other communities distinguish the chronology of events from the meanings narrators give them. In his methodological essay, voice, rhythm and narrative form matter, while an interview’s questions and circumstances help shape its answers. Errors in a remembered date can therefore become evidence about memory without replacing the established event chronology. His work combines oral history with literature and music scholarship.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Peculiarities of Oral History (1981); The Death of Luigi Trastulli and Other Stories: Form and Meaning in Oral History (1991); The Battle of Valle Giulia: Oral History and the Art of Dialogue (1997).

neighbor_nodes.scope_note: Halbwachs’s social frameworks, Nora’s commemorative sites, and Samuel’s popular uses of the past are distinct projects. Communicative and cultural memory are the Assmann project’s distinctions, not a universal taxonomy. War mourning, Holocaust memorials and feminist subjectivity require different historical explanations; this selection remains weighted toward European debates. Jelin’s Argentina project adds a pre-2000 case beyond Europe; it does not represent all Latin American memory work.

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering
strands.focus: Family, religious and class contexts organize recollection; a collective framework is not proof of one identical group memory.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); English selections (1992)

strands.title: Sites of memory and historical reconstruction
strands.focus: Sites combine material, symbolic and functional dimensions, extending beyond monuments alone.

strands.title: Habit, bodies and ceremony
strands.focus: Remembering includes bodily competence, not only recalled propositions or pictures.

strands.title: Communication and cultural objectivation
strands.focus: Everyday recollection and durable cultural forms operate differently; Assmann revises rather than merely repeats Halbwachs.

strands.title: Media and uses of cultural memory
strands.focus: Writing, images and monuments organize what can be stored and recalled.

strands.title: Mourning and cultural continuities after war
strands.focus: Traditional and modern forms overlap in Great War mourning; this is not a template for every subsequent catastrophe.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995)

strands.title: Holocaust memorials and their contexts
strands.focus: Memorial forms and meanings vary across places and institutions.

strands.title: Popular practices of historical knowledge
strands.focus: Family research, images and reenactment make historical work visible outside professional writing.

strands.title: Life histories, gender and subjectivity
strands.focus: Fascist everyday life and feminist psychoanalytic inquiry are distinct routes into interpreted recollection.

strands.title: Archival authority, access and inscription
strands.focus: Combe’s inquiry into access supplies a named resource to Derrida. His account differentiates archives from spontaneous memory and examines institutional authority and technical inscription. From the archival profession, Schwartz and Cook called archives 'active sites where social power is negotiated' whose appraisal and access shape collective memory (2002, abstract); the wider readership is on the entry archival_turn.

strands.title: Urban landscapes and public memory
strands.focus: Hayden’s collaborative practice links historical interpretation to lived places.

strands.title: Traditions in contact and conflict
strands.focus: Halbwachs explains revisions of collective remembering through contact with other groups and their traditions; social frameworks are not an assurance of a unanimous or unchanging past.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925), final concluding subsection

strands.title: Memorial production and public disagreement
strands.focus: Young’s Saarbrücken account follows a covert art project into public controversy and political recognition. His interpretation makes the memorial’s production and reception part of its meaning.
strands.works: Germany’s vanishing Holocaust monuments (1994), adapted extract

strands.title: Argentina: rights, remembrance and generations
strands.focus: Jelin examines competing public memories and tensions within human-rights activism. Her conclusion questions both political forgetting and repetition that prevents younger generations from reinterpreting the past.
strands.works: The Politics of Memory (1994), selected sections

strands.title: Vichy’s afterlife and historical inquiry
strands.focus: Rousso distinguishes memory as an object of research, as a preliminary examination of inherited representations, and as a way to extend an event’s historical study into its aftermath.
strands.works: Pour une histoire de la mémoire collective (1991), 163–166

strands.title: Jewish remembrance and historiography
strands.focus: Yerushalmi’s prologue asks why concern with historical meaning and remembrance need not give professional historical writing the central role. This is a situated historical question, not a timeless definition of Jewish people.

strands.title: Resources for studying forgetting
strands.focus: Jelin’s 1994 analysis explicitly draws on Yerushalmi’s transmission argument and Loraux’s treatment of amnesty and mourning. Their Spanish 1989 essays are distinct from Zakhor.
strands.works: Usos del olvido essays (1989), as used by Jelin (1994)

neighbor_nodes.label: Oral history
neighbor_nodes.description: Oral history creates and interprets testimony through interviews, archives and collaborative projects. Recorded accounts illuminate events, memory and narrative, while the interviewer, editing and social relations shape the evidence.
neighbor_nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Allan Nevins and Columbia’s Oral History Research Office (1948); Paul Thompson, The Voice of the Past (1978); Alessandro Portelli, The Death of Luigi Trastulli and Other Stories (1991).

strands.title: Recording lives and expanding evidence
strands.focus: Interviewing extends the range of historical testimony; access alone does not settle interpretation.
strands.works: Thompson, The Voice of the Past (1978)

strands.title: Narrative and the meanings of memory
strands.focus: Portelli separates what happened from what narrators make of it; discrepancies can require both factual checking and interpretation.

strands.title: Institutional collecting programmes
strands.focus: Nevins’s account links collection priorities to resources and projects, including a move beyond selected prominent individuals.

strands.title: Work, fascism and everyday negotiation
strands.focus: Memories of daily conduct complicate a simple division between consent and resistance.

strands.title: Feminist methodological questions
strands.focus: Feminist uses of interviews raise interpretive dilemmas rather than supplying one uniform method.

strands.title: Migration, gender and consciousness in South Africa
strands.focus: The Phokeng project connects life narratives, interviewing relationships and material conditions.

strands.title: Editing, audiences and public authority
strands.focus: Transcripts, films and museums make mediation itself a historical question.

strands.title: Transmitted traditions and interview evidence
strands.focus: Oral traditions require their own source criticism; neither source form belongs exclusively to one continent.

strands.title: Community participation and unequal representation
strands.focus: Thompson values community history while warning that participation alone can reproduce exclusions and comforting myths. Selection, listening and exchange of interpretation remain historical responsibilities.
strands.works: The Voice of the Past (1988), extracted community passage

strands.title: From recorded interview to public narrative
strands.focus: Frisch argues for accountable editing suited to audience and medium, retaining the original record while questioning literal transcription’s class effects. Rogovin’s photographs help frame Hughes’s interview; the printed demonstration is explicitly selective.

strands.title: Transmission, performance and recorded evidence
strands.focus: Vansina distinguishes eyewitness accounts from intergenerational traditions while recognizing communal circulation and feedback from writing. A recorded text is one performance within an ongoing tradition.
